Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe restoration of Israel.1–9Promises of guidance and happiness; Rachel lamenting.10–17Ephraim laments his errors.18–20The promised Saviour.21–26God's care over the church.27–34Peace and prosperity in gospel time.35–40
The Lord draws his people with everlasting love (verses 1–9)

God assured his people he would restore them to covenant fellowship with himself.

When we reach an unusually low condition and difficulties seem overwhelming, it helps to remember that the church has suffered greatly before.

Yet when we experience present displeasure, we find it hard to take comfort in past signs of God's favor.

For those who, through grace, share in the Lord's love, there is great happiness in knowing that it is everlasting love.

It has existed from eternity in God's purposes and continues forever in its effects.

Those whom he loves with this love he draws to himself through the work of the Holy Spirit within their souls.

When we praise the Lord for what he has already done, let us also ask him to grant what his church still needs and expects.

When God calls us, we should not claim that we cannot come.

The One who calls also helps and strengthens us.

His goodness leads people to repentance.

His redeemed people will weep over sin with deeper bitterness and tenderness after deliverance than they did when they were suffering under captivity.

If we receive God as our Father and join the church of the firstborn, we will lack nothing truly good for us.

Henry sees these promises as looking to a future gathering of Israel from every part of the world.

He also sees in their language a figurative description of sinners converted to Christ and led along a clear and safe path.

The scattered are gathered, and sorrow gives way to joy (verses 10–17)

The God who scattered Israel knows where every one of his people may be found.

His providential gifts give us abundant reason for gratitude.

But the soul is not a fruitful garden unless watered by the dew of his Spirit and grace.

The prophecy then makes a precious promise which, Henry says, will not find its full accomplishment apart from the heavenly Zion.

Those who know God's loving-kindness and are satisfied with it need no other blessing to make them truly happy.

Rachel is pictured as rising from her grave and refusing comfort because she believes her descendants have been destroyed.

The killing of Bethlehem's children by Herod (Matthew 2:16–18) fulfilled this prophecy to some degree, but Henry explicitly says it could not be its entire meaning.

If we have a secure hope of eternal inheritance, both for ourselves and those we love, we can endure temporal suffering—and God can make those troubles serve our good.

Ephraim repents and asks God to turn him (verses 18–20)

Ephraim, representing Israel's ten tribes, mourns sin.

He is angry with himself over wrongdoing, foolishness and stubborn rebellion.

He recognizes he cannot, by his own power, remain close to God—much less restore himself when he has wandered away.

Therefore he prays:

“Turn me, and I will be turned.”

His own will is brought into submission to God's.

When the Holy Spirit's teaching accompanied God's providential correction, the change was accomplished.

This is a comfort amid our suffering: the Lord has not forgotten us.

He has mercy reserved for everyone who seeks him sincerely—rich mercy, certain mercy and mercy fitted to their need.

The Savior prepares the road to freedom (verses 21–26)

The way from slavery to sin into the liberty of God's children is a highway.

It is both clear and safe.

Yet no one is likely to walk along it without deliberately setting the heart toward it.

The people receive encouragement from the promise of something new, unheard of and extraordinary—a creative work of almighty power.

Henry identifies it with the human nature of Jesus Christ, formed and prepared by the Holy Spirit's power.

He sees this as encouragement to the Jews to return to their land.

They were also promised a happy settlement there.

God has joined godliness with honesty.

No one may separate them or imagine that one can compensate for the absence of the other.

In the Lord's love and favor, the weary soul finds rest and the sorrowful find joy.

What could be more satisfying to see than Jerusalem's welfare and peace upon Israel?

The new covenant writes God's law upon the heart (verses 27–34)

God's people would become numerous and enjoy his blessing.

This passage is quoted in Hebrews 8:8–9 as the substance of the covenant of grace made with believers in Jesus Christ.

The promise is not that God will simply give people a different law.

Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it.

Rather, the same law that had been written on stone tablets will be written upon human hearts by the Holy Spirit.

Through grace the Lord will make his people willing to obey him.

Everyone will have the opportunity to know the Lord and receive the means of that knowledge.

When the gospel is proclaimed, the Holy Spirit will be poured out.

No person is finally destroyed except because of that person's own sins.

No one willing to receive Christ's salvation will be rejected.

God's covenant secures the future of his people (verses 35–40)

The sun, moon and other heavenly bodies will continue moving according to the order established by their Creator until time ends.

The roaring sea also remains under his authority.

Just as certainly, the Jews will continue to exist as a distinct people.

Henry says that scarcely any words could declare Israel's restoration more forcefully.

The rebuilding, enlargement and establishment of Jerusalem would be a pledge of the greater blessings God intended for the gospel church.

The future restoration of Israel, and every true believer's personal happiness, rest upon God's promise, covenant and oath.

His love surpasses knowledge.

Anyone who takes hold of that love receives every present mercy as a foretaste and pledge of salvation.

Chapter 31
The restoration of Israel. ( [Jer.31.1-Jer.31.9] Jr 31:1-9) Promises of guidance and happiness; Rachel lamenting. ( [Jer.31.10-Jer.31.17] Jr 31:10-17) Ephraim laments his errors. ( [Jer.31.18-Jer.31.20] Jr 31:18-20) The promised Saviour. ( [Jer.31.21-Jer.31.26] Jr 31:21-26) God's care over the church. ( [Jer.31.27-Jer.31.34] Jr 31:27-34) Peace and prosperity in gospel time. ( [Jer.31.35-Jer.31.40] Jr 31:35-40)
Verses 1-9 God assures his people that he will again take them into covenant relation to himself. When brought very low, and difficulties appear, it is good to remember that it has been so with the church formerly. But it is hard under present frowns to take comfort from former smiles; yet it is the happiness of those who, through grace, are interested in the love of God, that it is an everlasting love, from everlasting in the counsels, to everlasting in the continuance. Those whom God loves with this love, he will draw to himself, by the influences of his Spirit upon their souls. When praising God for what he has done, we must call upon him for the favours his church needs and expects. When the Lord calls, we must not plead that we cannot come; for he that calls us, will help us, will strengthen us. The goodness of God shall lead them to repentance. And they shall weep for sin with more bitterness, and more tenderness, when delivered out of their captivity, than when groaning under it. If we take God for our Father, and join the church of the first-born, we shall want nothing that is good for us. These predictions doubtless refer also to a future gathering of the Israelites from all quarters of the globe. And they figuratively describe the conversion of sinners to Christ, and the plain and safe way in which they are led.
[Jer.31.10-Jer.31.17]
Verses 10-17 He that scattered Israel, knows where to find them. It is comfortable to observe the goodness of the Lord in the gifts of providence. But our souls are never valuable as gardens, unless watered with the dews of God's Spirit and grace. A precious promise follows, which will not have full accomplishment except in the heavenly Zion. Let them be satisfied of God's loving-kindness, and they will be satisfied with it, and desire no more to make them happy. Rachel is represented as rising from her grave, and refusing to be comforted, supposing her offspring rooted out. The murder of the children at Bethlehem, by Herod, Matt. 2:16-18, in some degree fulfilled this prediction, but could not be its full meaning. If we have hope in the end, concerning an eternal inheritance, for ourselves and those belonging to us, all temporal afflictions may be borne, and will be for our good.
[Jer.31.18-Jer.31.20]
Verses 18-20 Ephraim (the ten tribes) is weeping for sin. He is angry at himself for his sin, and folly, and frowardness. He finds he cannot, by his own power, keep himself close with God, much less bring himself back when he is revolted. Therefore he prays, Turn thou me, and I shall be turned. His will was bowed to the will of God. When the teaching of God's Spirit went with the corrections of his providence, then the work was done. This is our comfort in affliction, that the Lord thinks upon us. God has mercy in store, rich mercy, sure mercy, suitable mercy, for all who seek him in sincerity.
[Jer.31.21-Jer.31.26]
Verses 21-26 The way from the bondage of sin to the liberty of God's children, is a high-way. It is plain, it is safe; yet none are likely to walk in it, unless they set their hearts towards it. They are encouraged by the promise of a new, unheard-of, extraordinary thing; a creation, a work of Almighty power; the human nature of Christ, formed and prepared by the power of the Holy Ghost: and this is here mentioned as an encouragement to the Jews to return to their own land. And a comfortable prospect is given them of a happy settlement there. Godliness and honesty God has joined: let no man think to put them asunder, or to make the one atone for the want of the other. In the love and favour of God the weary soul shall find rest, and the sorrowful shall find joy. And what can we see with more satisfaction than the good of Jerusalem, and peace upon Israel?
[Jer.31.27-Jer.31.34]
Verses 27-34 The people of God shall become numerous and prosperous. In Heb. 8:8,9, this place is quoted as the sum of the covenant of grace made with believers in Jesus Christ. Not, I will give them a new law; for Christ came not to destroy the law, but to fulfil it; but the law shall be written in their hearts by the finger of the Spirit, as formerly written in the tables of stone. The Lord will, by his grace, make his people willing people in the day of his power. All shall know the Lord; all shall be welcome to the knowledge of God, and shall have the means of that knowledge. There shall be an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, at the time the gospel is published. No man shall finally perish, but for his own sins; none, who is willing to accept of Christ's salvation.
[Jer.31.35-Jer.31.40]
Verses 35-40 As surely as the heavenly bodies will continue their settled course, according to the will of their Creator, to the end of time, and as the raging sea obeys him, so surely will the Jews be continued a separate people. Words can scarcely set forth more strongly the restoration of Israel. The rebuilding of Jerusalem, and its enlargement and establishment, shall be an earnest of the great things God will do for the gospel church. The personal happiness of every true believer, as well as the future restoration of Israel, is secured by promise, covenant, and oath. This Divine love passes knowledge; and to those who take hold upon it, every present mercy is an earnest of salvation.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJeremiah buys a field.1–15The prophet's prayer.16–25God declares that he will give up his people, but promises to restore them.26–44
Jeremiah buys land during the siege (verses 1–15)

Jeremiah was imprisoned because of his prophecies, yet he purchased a field.

That purchase was a sign.

Although Jerusalem was under siege and the land seemed about to be ruined, a time would return when people again bought and possessed houses, fields and vineyards.

Those who preach God's promises should demonstrate that they themselves believe what they teach.

Even our ordinary financial dealings and everyday business should be handled in faith, with attention to God's Providence and his promises.

Jeremiah prays to the sovereign and just God (verses 16–25)

The prophet worshiped the Lord for his infinite perfection.

Whenever we struggle to understand a particular way Providence is working, we should return to the truths that are most certain.

God is the source of all existence, power and life.

Nothing presents a difficulty too great for him to overcome.

He is a God of unlimited mercy.

He is also a God of uncompromising justice.

He directs everything according to what is best.

Jeremiah acknowledged God's righteousness in bringing judgment upon his people.

Whatever our situation, whether a personal trial or a public calamity, the Lord sees it and knows how to remedy it.

We should never quarrel with God's right to act.

But we may rightly ask to understand what his actions mean.

God's judgment and restoration both display his purposes (verses 26–44)

The Lord's answer revealed both his purposes of judgment against that generation and his purposes of mercy toward generations still to come.

Nothing but sin was responsible for the people's ruin.

Yet God promised the restoration of Judah and Jerusalem.

The people had finally fallen into despair.

The Lord answered by announcing mercy reserved for their future.

His promises are equally sure for everyone who truly believes.

He will acknowledge them as his people and show himself to be their God.

He will give them a heart that fears him.

All true Christians will possess a disposition to love one another.

They may differ in their views about lesser questions.

But they will be united in the great truths of God: the evil of sin; the low condition of fallen human beings; salvation through Jesus Christ; true holiness; the world's emptiness; and the importance of eternal things.

Those whom God loves, he loves to the end.

We have no reason to distrust his faithfulness or constancy.

We have every reason to be cautious about our own hearts.

He would settle the people again in Canaan.

Jeremiah's purchase was a pledge that many future purchases would follow the exile.

But those restored fields only faintly picture the inheritance reserved in the heavenly Canaan for people who fear God and persevere with him.

Let us therefore endure our trials, confident that he will accomplish all the good he has promised.

Jeremiah buys a field. ( [Jer.32.1-Jer.32.15] Jr 32:1-15) The prophet's prayer. ( [Jer.32.16-Jer.32.25] Jr 32:16-25) God declares that he will give up his people, but promises to restore them. ( [Jer.32.26-Jer.32.44] Jr 32:26-44)
Verses 1-15 Jeremiah, being in prison for his prophecy, purchased a piece of ground. This was to signify, that though Jerusalem was besieged, and the whole country likely to be laid waste, yet the time would come, when houses, and fields, and vineyards, should be again possessed. It concerns ministers to make it appear that they believe what they preach to others. And it is good to manage even our worldly affairs in faith; to do common business with reference to the providence and promise of God.
[Jer.32.16-Jer.32.25]
Verses 16-25 Jeremiah adores the Lord and his infinite perfections. When at any time we are perplexed about the methods of Providence, it is good for us to look to first principles. Let us consider that God is the fountain of all being, power, and life; that with him no difficulty is such as cannot be overcome; that he is a God of boundless mercy; that he is a God of strict justice; and that he directs every thing for the best. Jeremiah owns that God was righteous in causing evil to come upon them. Whatever trouble we are in, personal or public, we may comfort ourselves that the Lord sees it, and knows how to remedy it. We must not dispute God's will, but we may seek to know what it means.
[Jer.32.26-Jer.32.44]
Verses 26-44 God's answer discovers the purposes of his wrath against that generation of the Jews, and the purposes of his grace concerning future generations. It is sin, and nothing else, that ruins them. The restoration of Judah and Jerusalem is promised. This people were now at length brought to despair. But God gives hope of mercy which he had in store for them hereafter. Doubtless the promises are sure to all believers. God will own them for his, and he will prove himself theirs. He will give them a heart to fear him. All true Christians shall have a disposition to mutual love. Though they may have different views about lesser things, they shall all be one in the great things of God; in their views of the evil of sin, and the low estate of fallen man, the way of salvation through the Saviour, the nature of true holiness, the vanity of the world, and the importance of eternal things. Whom God loves, he loves to the end. We have no reason to distrust God's faithfulness and constancy, but only our own hearts. He will settle them again in Canaan. These promises shall surely be performed. Jeremiah's purchase was the pledge of many a purchase that should be made after the captivity; and those inheritances are but faint resemblances of the possessions in the heavenly Canaan, which are kept for all who have God's fear in their hearts, and do not depart from him. Let us then bear up under our trials, assured we shall obtain all the good he has promised us.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe restoration of the Jews.1–13The Messiah promised; happiness of his times.14–26
God promises restoration and peace (verses 1–13)

Those who expect comfort from God must call upon him.

His promises are not given to replace prayer, but to awaken and encourage it.

These promises lead us to the gospel of Christ. In the gospel, God reveals truth to guide us and peace to give our hearts rest.

His sanctifying grace cleanses sinners from the corruption of sin, and his forgiving mercy frees them from its guilt.

When people are thus justified, washed and sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Holy Spirit, they are enabled to walk before God in peace and purity.

Many observers then recognize the difference between God's people and the surrounding world, and they come to fear his righteous judgment.

The Lord promises that people who have endured sorrow for a long time will again be filled with joy.

Where he gives righteousness and peace, he also supplies what is necessary for earthly needs. All the things we possess become genuine comforts as they are sanctified through his word and prayer.

The promised Messiah and his eternal kingdom (verses 14–26)

To complete the promised blessings, God gives the promise of the Messiah.

Christ gives his church righteousness. God has made him our righteousness, and in him believers become the righteousness of God.

Christ is our Lord God, our righteousness, our sanctification and our redemption.

His kingdom will never end.

In this world, however, prosperity and adversity alternate like light and darkness, day and night.

God will also establish the covenant concerning the priesthood.

All true believers form a holy and royal priesthood. They offer spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God, beginning with themselves as living sacrifices.

The covenant promises will find their complete fulfillment in the Israel of the gospel.

According to Galatians 6:16, those who walk according to the gospel's rule belong to the Israel of God, upon whom are peace and mercy.

Yet we must not despise the families who were God's chosen people in ancient times, even though for a season they appear to have been set aside.

Verses 1-13 Those who expect to receive comforts from God, must call upon him. Promises are given, not to do away, but to quicken and encourage prayer. These promises lead us to the gospel of Christ; and in that God has revealed truth to direct us, and peace to make us easy. All who by sanctifying grace are cleansed from the filth of sin, by pardoning mercy are freed from the guilt. When sinners are thus justified, washed, and sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Holy Spirit, they are enabled to walk before God in peace and purity. Many are led to perceive the real difference between the people of God and the world around them, and to fear the Divine wrath. It is promised that the people who were long in sorrow, shall again be filled with joy. Where the Lord gives righteousness and peace, he will give all needful supplies for temporal wants; and all we have will be comforts, as sanctified by the word and by prayer.
[Jer.33.14-Jer.33.26]
Verses 14-26 To crown the blessings God has in store, here is a promise of the Messiah. He imparts righteousness to his church, for he is made of God to us righteousness; and believers are made the righteousness of God in him. Christ is our Lord God, our righteousness, our sanctification, and our redemption. His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. But in this world prosperity and adversity succeed each other, as light and darkness, day and night. The covenant of priesthood shall be secured. And all true believers are a holy priesthood, a royal priesthood, they offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God; themselves, in the first place, as living sacrifices. The promises of that covenant shall have full accomplishment in the gospel Israel. In Gal. 6:16, all that walk according to the gospel rule, are made to be the Israel of God, on whom shall be peace and mercy. Let us not despise the families which were of old the chosen people of God, though for a time they seem to be cast off.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesZedekiah's death at Babylon foretold.1–7The Jews reproved for compelling their poor brethren to return to unlawful bondage.8–22
Zedekiah is warned of his captivity (verses 1–7)

Zedekiah learned that Jerusalem would fall and that he would die in captivity.

Nevertheless, his death would be natural, not an execution.

It is better to live and die repentant in a prison than to live and die unrepentant in a palace.

The people force their freed servants back into bondage (verses 8–22)

Under Israel's law, an Israelite was not to remain in this kind of service beyond the appointed period of seven years.

The people and their ancestors had violated that obligation.

They finally released their servants, but when it seemed possible that the siege might be lifted, they forced the people they had freed back into servitude.

People who try to deceive God with pretended repentance and incomplete reform end up deceiving themselves most of all.

Imagining that they are free to sin merely gives them the freedom to expose themselves to the most severe judgments.

When we disappoint God's rightful expectations that we will do our duty, he may justly disappoint our expectation of receiving mercy.

A reform motivated only by terror seldom lasts.

Solemn promises made to God and then deliberately broken profane his appointed ordinances.

Those most eager to bind themselves with an appeal to God's name may also be the quickest to violate their own promises.

Let us examine our hearts so that our repentance is genuine, and let God's law govern how we act.

Chapter 34
Zedekiah's death at Babylon foretold. ( [Jer.34.1-Jer.34.7] Jr 34:1-7) The Jews reproved for compelling their poor brethren to return to unlawful bondage. ( [Jer.34.8-Jer.34.22] Jr 34:8-22)
Verses 1-7 Zedekiah is told that the city shall be taken, and that he shall die a captive, but he shall die a natural death. It is better to live and die penitent in a prison, than to live and die impenitent in a palace.
[Jer.34.8-Jer.34.22]
Verses 8-22 A Jew should not be held in servitude above seven years. This law they and their fathers had broken. And when there was some hope that the siege was raised, they forced the servants they had released into their services again. Those who think to cheat God by dissembled repentance and partial reformation, put the greatest cheat upon their own souls. This shows that liberty to sin, is really only liberty to have the sorest judgments. It is just with God to disappoint expectations of mercy, when we disappoint the expectations of duty. And when reformation springs only from terror, it is seldom lasting. Solemn vows thus entered into, profane the ordinances of God; and the most forward to bind themselves by appeals to God, are commonly most ready to break them. Let us look to our hearts, that our repentance may be real, and take care that the law of God regulates our conduct.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe obedience of the Rechabites.1–11The Jews' disobedience to the Lord.12–19
The Rechabites obey their ancestor (verses 1–11)

Jonadab was known for wisdom and godliness. He had lived almost three hundred years earlier; his life is also mentioned in 2 Kings 10:15.

Jonadab had instructed his descendants not to drink wine.

He also directed them to live in tents or movable dwellings, which would teach them not to regard any earthly place as their permanent home.

Remaining humble and content was the safest way for them to continue living in the land as strangers.

Humility and contentment are always wise and are often the best protection people can have.

Jonadab wanted his descendants to avoid unlawful pleasures. He therefore taught them to deny themselves even certain pleasures that were lawful in themselves.

Since we are strangers and pilgrims in the world, we should abstain from sinful bodily desires.

Those with little to lose will fear times of loss less. People who do not cling tightly to possessions will find it easier to surrender them if they are taken away.

Those best prepared to endure hardship practice self-denial and regard worldly vanities as unimportant.

The descendants of Jonadab faithfully followed the rules he had given them.

They made exceptions only where ordinary precautions were necessary for their safety during a time of widespread danger.

Their obedience exposes Judah's disobedience (verses 12–19)

The Rechabites' faithfulness was tested as a sign.

Their obedience highlighted the much greater disobedience of the Jews toward God.

The Rechabites had obeyed a man who was only a human being like themselves.

Jonadab had never done for his descendants what God had done for his people.

The Lord promised blessing to the Rechabites.

Scripture does not report how that promise was fulfilled. Henry expressed confidence that it was fulfilled and noted reports by travelers that a distinct Rechabite people could still be found in his own era. That report is a historical claim of the commentator, not an independently established identification.

Let us heed the godly advice of faithful predecessors. It is good to follow their wise counsel.
classic_reading:
[Jer.35.1-Jer.35.11]
Chapter 35
The obedience of the Rechabites. ( [Jer.35.1-Jer.35.11] Jr 35:1-11) The Jews' disobedience to the Lord. ( [Jer.35.12-Jer.35.19] Jr 35:12-19)
Verses 1-11 Jonadab was famous for wisdom and piety. He lived nearly 300 years before, II Kin. 10:15. Jonadab charged his posterity not to drink wine. He also appointed them to dwell in tents, or movable dwelling: this would teach them not to think of settling any where in this world. To keep low, would be the way to continue long in the land where they were strangers. Humility and contentment are always the best policy, and men's surest protection. Also, that they might not run into unlawful pleasures, they were to deny themselves even lawful delights. The consideration that we are strangers and pilgrims should oblige us to abstain from all fleshly lusts. Let them have little to lose, and then losing times would be the less dreadful: let them sit loose to what they had, and then they might with less pain be stript of it. Those are in the best frame to meet sufferings who live a life of self-denial, and who despise the vanities of the world. Jonadab's posterity observed these rules strictly, only using proper means for their safety in a time of general suffering.
[Jer.35.12-Jer.35.19]
Verses 12-19 The trial of the Rechabites' constancy was for a sign; it made the disobedience of the Jews to God the more marked. The Rechabites were obedient to one who was but a man like themselves, and Jonadab never did for his seed what God has done for his people. Mercy is promised to the Rechabites. We are not told respecting the performance of this promise; but doubtless it was performed, and travellers say the Rechabites may be found a separate people to this day. Let us follow the counsels of our pious forefathers, and we shall find good in so doing.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesBaruch is to write the prophecies of Jeremiah.1–8The princes advise them to hide themselves.9–19The king having heard a part, burns the roll.20–32
Baruch writes Jeremiah's prophecies (verses 1–8)

God himself directed that the Scriptures should be written down.

His wisdom appointed writing as an appropriate means of warning the people.

If the warning failed to change them, Judah would have still less excuse for refusing to listen.

The Lord announces judgment against sinners so that they may hear, fear and turn away from their evil ways.

Whenever anyone responds to his warnings in this way, trusting in his promised mercy, the Lord is ready to forgive their sins.

Those who refuse are left without excuse.

The seriousness of God's anger against our sin ought to stir us both to prayer and to earnest efforts to obey him.

The officials hear the scroll (verses 9–19)

Outward displays of reverence and devotion may be found among people who keep up the forms of religion but remain strangers—even enemies—to its living power.

The officials listened patiently as the whole scroll was read.

They became deeply afraid.

Yet even people convinced that a message is true and important, and inclined to help those who preach it, may still hesitate because of concerns about their safety, their personal interests or their prospects for advancement.

Such reservations can keep them from acting according to what their consciences know.

They may even try to dismiss the disturbing truth rather than obey it.

The king burns the scroll (verses 20–32)

Those who despise God's word may soon show that they hate it.

Like the king who burned the scroll, they would like to see the word itself destroyed.

This reveals the deep hostility of the sinful human mind toward God, and should make us marvel at his patience.

The officials had shown some concern about the warning.

Yet when they saw how lightly the king treated it, their own concern weakened.

Do not treat God's word as something trivial.

All others will be left without excuse; and the consideration that great is the anger God has pronounced against us for sin, should quicken both our prayers and our endeavours.

Many people see the deadly consequences of someone else's sins, yet carelessly step into that person's place and follow the same destructive course.

When we are in trouble, we should seek the prayers of ministers and Christian friends.

A temporary pause in judgment may even make sinners more stubborn.

Whatever instruments he has determined to use will fulfill his purpose, even if they appear unlikely to succeed.

At times the wise course for godly people is to withdraw, enter their rooms and shut their doors (Isaiah 26:20).

Jeremiah was arrested as if he were deserting to the enemy, and he was thrown into prison.

It is nothing new for those who most faithfully serve the church to be falsely accused of secretly helping its worst enemies.

When such charges are made, we may deny them and entrust our case to the God who judges righteously.

The Lord gave Jeremiah grace to remain faithful.

He would not purchase a human ruler's mercy by betraying either God or his rightful duty toward the king.

He told the king the entire truth.

When speaking God's message, Jeremiah was bold.

When presenting his own request, he was humble and respectful.

A lion in God's cause should be a lamb in his own.

God gave Jeremiah favor in the king's eyes.

The Lord can even turn a prison cell into pasture for his people and raise up friends to provide for them.

He can feed them even during famine.

Jeremiah is imprisoned and rescued (verses 1–13)

Jeremiah continued to preach God's word plainly, just as the officials continued in their malice.

Wicked people commonly regard faithful ministers as enemies because those ministers show them how much harm they are doing to themselves by refusing repentance.

Jeremiah was thrown into a dungeon.

Many faithful witnesses for God have died quietly and unnoticed in prisons.

But Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian, spoke courageously and truthfully to the king: the men who had dealt with Jeremiah had acted wickedly.

Notice how God can raise up friends to help his people in the deepest distress.

The king ordered Jeremiah's release, and Ebed-melech saw that the prophet was pulled out of the dungeon.

His particular tenderness toward Jeremiah deserves attention.

This should encourage us to stand openly for God.

In these opposing characters, we recognize an enduring difference: God's children become like their Father, while Satan's children imitate their master.

Jeremiah advises Zedekiah to surrender (verses 14–28)

Jeremiah was reluctant to repeat warnings that appeared only to endanger his own life and increase the king's guilt.

Yet he pressed Zedekiah with the truth and challenged the fear that held him back from obedience to God.

The less people fear God, the more they tend to fear other people.

They often lack the courage to act according to their own judgments and consciences, even when they know what is right.

Jerusalem is captured (verses 1–10)

Jerusalem was so strongly fortified that its inhabitants believed no enemy could ever enter it.

But the people's sins provoked God to withdraw his protection.

Without him, the city was just as vulnerable as any other.

Zedekiah's eyes were put out.

A man who had shut his eyes to the clear light of God's word was now condemned to literal darkness.

Those who refuse to believe what God says will eventually be convinced when his words are fulfilled.

Notice the astonishing changes of Providence.

Earthly possessions and circumstances are never secure.

The Lord's judgments are just.

But whether he makes people rich or poor, neither condition will do them real good while they cling to their sins.

Jeremiah receives kind treatment (verses 11–14)

God's faithful servants are the people best prepared for whatever may happen.

Even while wicked people suffer, those who belong to God may experience rescue and comfort.

They sometimes receive more kindness from people who make no profession of religion than from people who outwardly claim to be godly.

The Lord can raise up friends for his people, do them good and fulfill every one of his promises.

Ebed-melech receives a promise of safety (verses 15–18)

God sent a message to assure Ebed-melech that his great kindness toward Jeremiah would be rewarded.

The reason for the promise was explicit: “Because you have trusted in me,” says the Lord.

God regards not only the outward service people perform, but the faith and motives from which they act.

Those who trust him while doing their duty, as Ebed-melech did, will discover that their hope does not fail even amid the greatest danger.

Jeremiah is free to join Gedaliah (verses 1–6)

The commander of the guard seemed almost proud to have served as the instrument through which God fulfilled what Jeremiah had been sent to announce.

Many people readily recognize God's justice and truth in what happens to others, yet remain blind and careless about their own sins.

Sooner or later, everyone must see that sin is the cause of human misery.

Jeremiah was allowed to choose where to go.

He was advised to join Gedaliah, the governor appointed over the land under Babylon's king.

Henry expresses uncertainty about whether Jeremiah made the best decision in accepting this advice.

Yet people who sincerely seek sinners' salvation and the good of the church may look for signs of better days where others see very little hope.

They often prefer an opportunity to do useful work to a safer position where they cannot serve others.

A plot against Gedaliah (verses 7–16)

Jeremiah had never promised that the Jews would enjoy good times immediately following the captivity.

Yet the circumstances briefly seemed to offer hope.

How quickly that prospect was destroyed!

When God begins a judgment, he will accomplish what he intends.

So long as pride, ambition and revenge rule people's hearts, they will continually devise new schemes and stir up trouble, usually bringing ruin upon themselves.

Who would have expected another rebellion so soon after Jerusalem's destruction?

Human nature does not become good simply because it has endured great suffering.

Only God's grace can bring real change.

Even if those imprisoned for final judgment were allowed to return to earth, their hearts would still be wicked unless their nature was renewed.

Lord, give us new hearts and the new mind that comes with new birth.

You have said that without this new birth we cannot enter your heavenly kingdom.
